description:
Jesteśmy RAM-pam-pam – paczką studentów Informatyki Geoprzestrzennej. W wyzwaniu "Dancing with the SARs" wykorzystujemy dane radarowe NISAR (pasmo L) do wykrywania niewidzialnych deformacji infrastruktury pod okapem lasu.

Nasze skille: GIS, InSAR, Google Earth Engine, Python, C++, React & FastAPI.

Kogo szukamy (Status): 🚨 ZESPÓŁ JEST PEŁNY 🚨 Mamy już komplet i nie rekrutujemy nowych członków.
summary: Corridor Watch is an interactive platform for exploring satellite-observed ground movement near critical infrastructure. It brings together 2D maps, 3D terrain models, time-series visualizations, and infrastructure layers for three study areas: Tabasco, Portuguese Bend, and Bayou Corne. Users can follow changes across available observation dates, inspect areas of concern, and explore nearby pipelines, roads, railways, buildings, and other features. By making complex Earth-observation results easier to interpret in their geographic context, the project helps users identify locations that may warrant further investigation. It is designed as a decision-support and communication tool—not as a substitute for field inspection or engineering assessment. The project demonstrates how satellite data and geospatial visualization can support more informed monitoring of communities and infrastructure exposed to ground instability.
details:
Corridor Watch presents geospatial data for three areas of interest through an interactive web application. Users can switch between a 2D, top-down view and a 3D terrain model, explore available observation dates on a timeline, and turn map layers on or off. In Portuguese Bend, the application brings NISAR InSAR displacement results into context with buildings and infrastructure such as roads, railways, and pipelines. In Tabasco, users can inspect ground-motion time series, pipeline-related anomalies, analysis profiles, and a GNSS reference station. Bayou Corne is included as a 3D terrain and sinkhole case study.

The project uses a JavaScript frontend with Three.js for 3D visualization and a Python backend built with FastAPI. Its data and processing workflows use geospatial sources and formats including InSAR, GeoJSON, satellite and aerial imagery, elevation data, and infrastructure layers. By combining these sources in one interface, Corridor Watch makes it easier to explore where observed ground movement overlaps with infrastructure and which areas may merit follow-up. It is intended to support awareness and further investigation, not to predict failures or certify structural damage. The team considered data coverage, uncertainty, time periods, and the need to distinguish ground movement from the condition of an asset.
